claims.text: Superior dynamic strength–ductility behavior in high-entropy alloys arises from an interplay between chemical short-range order and lattice distortion.
Chemical short-range order increases resistance to screw-dislocation motion.
The increased resistance to screw-dislocation motion is caused by diffuse antiphase boundaries and the energetic cost of breaking chemical order.
Chemical short-range order promotes easier glide of edge dislocations.
Inherent lattice distortion enhances edge-dislocation mobility in high-entropy alloys.
Differential effects on screw and edge dislocations enhance work hardening under dynamic loading without sacrificing ductility.
Annealing can produce different degrees of short-range order while grain size and other microstructural features are held constant.
Rapid quenching produces a nearly fully disordered high-entropy-alloy baseline with minimal short-range order.
Enhanced short-range order will increase dynamic yield strength relative to the quenched disordered baseline.
Enhanced short-range order will increase strain-rate sensitivity relative to the disordered baseline.
Enhanced short-range order will maintain or improve total tensile ductility relative to the disordered baseline.
Enhanced short-range order will produce greater dynamic work-hardening rates.
Enhanced short-range order will delay necking under dynamic loading.
The proposed mechanism applies to refractory BCC high-entropy alloys with significant lattice distortion and a tendency toward chemical ordering.
The proposed mechanism also applies to equiatomic FCC high-entropy alloys.
The mechanism should operate below or near the order–disorder transition temperature and become non-dominant far above that temperature.
The strengthening contribution of short-range order to screw-dislocation motion decreases as temperature increases.
Dynamic recovery and secondary phases may alter the measured contribution of short-range order.
